Q: Crazy attempt: I want to crack the system of Casio electronic dictionary (reverse engineering) and turn it into a real "computer" A:

First thing you must get working is to be able to compiled the decompiled code without making any changes to it or even understanding it. Then you need to successfully deploy the result on your target system and have it behave as expected.

If you can't do any of that, there is very little hope of success.

Once you've managed those two steps: You just edit the decompiled code with a regular editor. Understanding the code may be necessary at this time but you could make simple changes, like changing some textual output, like a greeting message if there is one.

Then you compile and deploy again. If you are lucky, it's accepted by the target.

Q: Is minifying of CSS classes names across the razor files, css files and c# files possible? A:

I think that the CSS selectors in JS are used as strings. But strings can have anything in them without specific context. Therefore theoretically it is not possible to distinguish which one of those will be used as a selector that needs to be minified.

Q: Term::ReadLine - I need to hit the up arrow twice to retrieve history A:

It is worth noting that an an alternative option would be to disable the autohistory feature in the ReadLine module, rather than removing $term->addhistory() from your code.

This can be done by adding the following lines to your script:

# This disables autohistory
$term->MinLine(MAX);

In certain circumstances, this may be preferable, as you may wish to use a different history method for greater control over the history, or for whatever reason.

For instance, if you use Term::UI then you probably want to use the history method provided by Term::UI, and will need to disable the ReadLine auto-history feature, otherwise you end up with duplicate entries in the history, for each input entered.

In fact, I came across this question when trying to fix the duplicate history entries, whilst using the code from the synopsis of Term::UI .

Related

  • Term::ReadLine::Gnu vs. history control
  • The synopsis should probably show the disabling of the autohistory in ReadLine #21

Q: How to cryptographically prove a file existed at a specific time? A:

Many certificate authorities also have an adjacent "trusted time-stamping" service, where instead of signing a certificate, they sign a provided hash of some arbitrary data. The signature is verifiable using the TSA's certificate chain.

Specifically, such timestamping services are commonly used for Authenticode signing (i.e. signing Windows .exe files) – the timestamp service's counter-signature is what prevents a signed .exe from suddenly becoming invalid the next year when the developer's certificate expires.

(You can right-click an .exe and go to "Digital Signatures > Details" to see the counter-signature with the CA's timestamp in addition to the signer's self-asserted timestamp.)

For example, DigiCert and Sectigo provide public TSA services, as do Apple and Microsoft – all nominally for code-signing purposes but they don't really care what hash you give them. The service uses the RFC 3161 protocol and you can use openssl ts to generate the requests or verify the returned timestamps.

Similar services are also used for eIDAS "qualified document signing" in the XAdES/PAdES/CAdES specifications, where you have a whole set of specifications detailing what kind of auxiliary data (e.g. certificate chains, OCSP responses) must be bundled together with the document to make it fully verifiable offline two decades later.

I don't know if that's common elsewhere in the world, but in my corner of Europe a "digitally-signed contract" would come either as a PAdES-format signed PDF document, or a plain PDF in a XAdES format archive, either way with the timestamp and all verification metadata (both for the signer and for the TSA) bundled in the document.

The ¤AdES formats are complex (and the "qualified" timestamping services generally paid-access), but they are a wheel already invented – so if you actually want to timestamp a contract, I'd strongly recommend first looking into whether any such format has already been adopted in your region or jurisdiction or whatever.

Q: Why is PostgreSQL TRUNCATE table MVCC unsafe A:

A “why” question!

There is a pretty good explanation in the commit message of the commit that updated the documentation to its current wording:

The table-rewriting forms of ALTER TABLE are MVCC-unsafe, in much the same way as TRUNCATE, because they replace all rows of the table with newly-made rows with a new xmin. (Ideally, concurrent transactions with old snapshots would continue to see the old table contents, but the data is not there anymore --- and if it were there, it would be inconsistent with the table's updated rowtype, so there would be serious implementation problems to fix.)
